# tokens: # word / __SP splice marker
# `word <value>` wraps its (unevaluated) argument in an internal __SP
# splice marker. When the marker reaches the stack pointer it is
# replaced by its payload and re-stepped against the LIVE stack:
#   - a plain list contributes its top-level elements (so a word-bearing
#     list runs as a Forth-style macro),
#   - any other value contributes itself.
# `def name word value` binds the marker, giving an explicit splice
# (the type-agnostic counterpart of the implicit `def name [list]`
# splice, which is unchanged). In a forward-argument position a
# DATA-splice-bound word expands like the written paren group —
# f w ≡ f (w) — see §7. Expected values use the canon renderer
# (containers are space-separated).
# 1. Standalone `word`: scalar splices itself, list splices its elements
word 42
note: a scalar splices as a single value
a plain list splices its top-level elements

# tokens: word [] 9
note: an empty list contributes nothing
only the top level splices; inner lists stay values

# tokens: # 2. Macro: spliced words execute against the live stack
5 word [dup add]
note: dup add run against the caller's 5 -> 10

# tokens: 1 2 word [add] 10
note: spliced `add` forward-collects the trailing 10: 2 add 10 = 12

# tokens: # 3. def name word value — binds the splice marker
# FORWARD form only. `word`'s __SP must be collected as def's forward
# argument (the pointer skips a collected arg, so the marker does not
# fire). There is NO prefix-form splice — `[body] def name` puts the
# body on the stack BEFORE def, so the pointer steps (and fires) any
# marker before def consumes it; a prefix list body therefore binds the
# list VALUE. `quote` can't ferry the marker either: `quote (word …)`
# fires the __SP inside the paren before quote marks it, and `quote
# word …` captures the literal token `word` as an atom. Use the forward
# form below for splices; use prefix only for value binding.
def doub word [dup add] 5 doub
note: explicit splice-macro (cf. implicit def doub [dup add])

# tokens: def p word [1 add 2] [p]

# tokens: # 7. Forward-argument positions: f w ≡ f (w) for DATA splices
# A word bound to a DATA splice (payload holds only values — no words,
# parens, or reaches at the top level) occupies a forward-argument
# position exactly as the written paren group (w) would: the payload's
# values arrive in place, a multi-value splice fills several slots, an
# empty splice contributes nothing. This is the JS-spread call form:
# Three exemptions keep their existing semantics:
#   - /q and raw-capture slots take the word/token itself, binding
#     notwithstanding (quote vs captures the NAME — see §3);
#   - CODE-bearing splices ([1 add], [dup add]) are Forth-style macros
#     that run against the LIVE stack; paren isolation would change
#     their meaning, so they stay boundary words in forward scans.
#     Group explicitly — f (p) — to use a code splice's result;
#   - BINDERS alias: def's value slot collects the marker itself, so
#     `def y xs` makes y the same splice (rebinding = aliasing).
#     Write `def y (xs)` to force expansion at a binder.
def vs word [2,3] def add2 fn [[x:Integer y:Integer][Integer][x add y]] add2 vs
note: multi-value data splice fills both forward slots
